header_title: One Sentence Holds All of Chemistry
audio_script: If, in some cataclysm, all of scientific knowledge were to be destroyed, and only one sentence passed on to the next generations, what statement would carry the most information in the fewest words? I believe it is the atomic hypothesis that all things are made of atoms. Little particles that move around in perpetual motion, attracting each other when they are a little distance apart, but repelling upon being squeezed into one another. In that one sentence there is an enormous amount of information about the world, if just a little imagination and thinking are applied. The atoms are one or two times ten to the minus eight centimeters in radius. That length is called an angstrom. If an apple were magnified to the size of the earth, the atoms in the apple would be about the size of the original apple. Look at a drop of water, a quarter of an inch on a side. Magnify it a billion times. Suddenly you see a teeming crowd of little balls jiggling, bouncing, sticking together. Black blobs are oxygen, white blobs are hydrogen, each oxygen holding two hydrogens. They attract when a little apart, repel when squeezed. The jiggling is heat. Heat it more and the molecules fly apart into steam. Cool it and they lock into a rigid pattern, ice. Everything is made of atoms. That is the key hypothesis. The most important idea in all of biology is that everything animals do, atoms do. Nothing living does anything that cannot be understood from the point of view that we are made of atoms acting according to the laws of physics.

header_title: Energy Is a Strange Kind of Counting
tagline: The most important law is a bookkeeping rule
audio_script: There is a fact, or if you wish a law, governing all natural phenomena that are known to date. There is no known exception. The law is called the conservation of energy. It says that there is a certain quantity, which we call energy, that does not change in the manifold changes which nature undergoes. That is a most abstract idea. It is not a description of a mechanism. It is just a strange fact that we can calculate some number, and when we finish watching nature go through her tricks and calculate the number again, it is the same. Imagine a child, Dennis the Menace, who has twenty-eight indestructible blocks. His mother counts them at the beginning of the day and again at the end. Always twenty-eight. One day she finds only twenty-seven, but a block is under the rug. Another day twenty-six, but two went out the window. Then thirty, because Bruce came and left some. She learns to look everywhere. She closes the window, keeps Bruce out, and the number stays constant. Then she finds twenty-five, but the toy box is heavy. She weighs the box. She discovers a formula. Then the water in the bathtub changes level. Another term. She invents term after term for places she cannot see. So it is with energy. The most remarkable aspect is that there are no blocks. Energy has a large number of different forms, gravitational, kinetic, heat, elastic, electrical, chemical, radiant, nuclear, mass. If we total up all the formulas for each, the sum does not change except for energy going in or out. In physics today, we have no knowledge of what energy is. We do not have a picture that energy comes in little blobs. It is an abstract thing. But when we add all the formulas, we always get twenty-eight.

header_title: What Is Time? It Is How Long We Wait
audio_script: What is time? It would be nice if we could find a good definition. Webster defines a time as a period, and a period as a time, which is not useful. Perhaps we should say, time is what happens when nothing else happens. Which also does not get us far. Maybe it is just as well to face the fact that time is one of the things we probably cannot define in the dictionary sense, and just say it is what we already know it to be. It is how long we wait. What matters is not how we define time but how we measure it. One way is to use something that happens over and over in a regular fashion, something periodic. A day is one such thing. We compare it against another, like an hourglass. We find that the number of hours from noon to noon is the same, and we gain confidence. Now we want smaller intervals. Galileo noticed that a pendulum swings back and forth in equal times, as long as the swing is small. If a given pendulum oscillates thirty-six hundred times in one hour, we call each period a second. We have divided our original unit into a hundred thousand pieces. And we can keep going. Electrical oscillators replace pendulums. We compare fast against slow, calibrating each against the next. Today, the best clock in the world is an atomic clock, based on the vibration of the cesium atom. One second is nine billion, one hundred ninety-two million, six hundred thirty-one thousand, seven hundred seventy cycles of that vibration. Not of a pendulum. Not of a quartz crystal. Of the atom. Time is what a periodic event measures. That is all we know.

header_title: How Far Does a Drunken Sailor Get?
audio_script: Imagine a drunken sailor comes out of a bar and takes a sequence of steps. Each step is chosen at an arbitrary angle, at random, determined by the toss of a coin. The question is, after a long time, where is he? Of course we do not know. It is impossible to say. But on the average, how far away from the bar has he gone? This problem is closely related to the motion of atoms in a gas, called Brownian motion, and to the combination of errors in measurements. First, let us ask how far he gets on the average. His average progress is zero, since he is equally likely to go either forward or backward. But we feel that as he takes more steps, he is more likely to have strayed farther from the starting point. So we ask for the average of the square of the distance. After one step, D squared is always one. After N steps, the expected value of D squared is just N. Not N squared. N. The root-mean-square distance is the square root of N. In thirty steps, we expect a typical distance of about five and a half, in units of the step length. If the sailor takes ten thousand steps, he ends up about one hundred step-lengths from the bar. Not ten thousand. One hundred. This is why a tiny particle jiggling in water, bombarded by molecules, spreads out slowly. It is the same mathematics. If you open a bottle of perfume in a room, the molecules diffuse, but they take the square root of the number of collisions to get anywhere. Randomness is not fast. It is slow. But it always gets there in the end, as the square root of the number of steps.

tagline: One law explains planets and apples
audio_script: In this lecture we discuss one of the most far-reaching generalizations of the human mind. The law of gravitation: every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force proportional to the mass of each, and varying inversely as the square of the distance between them. That is the whole law. Add the fact that an object responds to a force by accelerating in the direction of the force, by an amount inversely proportional to its mass, and you have said everything required. A sufficiently talented mathematician could then deduce all the consequences. The story begins with the ancients observing the planets, and Copernicus saying they go around the sun. Tycho Brahe measured their positions for many years. Kepler studied his tables and found three laws. First, each planet moves in an ellipse, with the sun at one focus. Second, the radius vector sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Third, the squares of the periods are proportional to the cubes of the semi-major axes. Newton, studying the laws of motion, realized the sun could be the seat of forces that govern the planets. He showed that the fact of equal areas is a sign post of forces directed exactly toward the sun. From Kepler's third law, he deduced that the force varies inversely as the square of the distance. Being a man of considerable feeling for generalities, he supposed this applied more generally than just to the sun holding the planets. Everything pulls everything. The next test was whether the pull of the earth on its people was the same as its pull on the moon. If an object near the surface falls sixteen feet in the first second, how far does the moon fall in the same time? The answer turns out to be roughly one-twentieth of an inch. That fits beautifully with the inverse-square law. Newton made his calculations very carefully, found a discrepancy, and did not publish. Six years later, a new measurement of the earth's size corrected his numbers, and the agreement was perfect.

header_title: Speed Is a Limit, Not a Ratio
audio_script: How do we define the speed of a moving object? A lady is caught by a cop. He says, lady, you were going sixty miles an hour. She says, that's impossible, I was travelling for only seven minutes. How can I go sixty miles an hour when I wasn't going an hour? The cop would say, tell that to the judge. But let us try to answer her honestly. What we mean, lady, is this: if you kept on going the same way you are going now, in the next hour you would go sixty miles. She says, well, my foot was off the accelerator and the car was slowing down. So if I kept on going that way, it would not go sixty miles. Or consider the falling ball. We want the speed at three seconds. Suppose we ask how far it falls between three and three point one seconds. We compute the distance at three point one, subtract the distance at three, divide by zero point one. That gives us an average speed over that interval. It is close to the speed at three, but not exact. We do better by taking a shorter interval, one thousandth of a second. Then one millionth. The result gets closer and closer. The exact speed is the limit of the distance travelled divided by the time required, as the time goes to zero. This idea was invented by Newton and by Leibniz, independently. It is the beginning of the differential calculus. Calculus was invented to describe motion. Its first application was to the problem of defining what is meant by going sixty miles an hour. When we say the ball falls sixteen t squared, we can differentiate and find that the speed is thirty-two t. At five seconds, the ball is going one hundred sixty feet per second. Not one hundred forty-four, which the average over the fifth second would suggest. Precisely one hundred sixty. That is what the derivative gives you.

header_title: The Rules of the Cosmic Game
audio_script: Before Newton, the motions of things like the planets were a mystery. After Newton, there was complete understanding. The motions of pendulums, oscillators with springs and weights, and so on, could all be analyzed. The next thing needed, after Galileo's principle of inertia, was a rule for how an object changes its speed when something is affecting it. That was Newton's contribution. He wrote down three laws. The first is inertia, restated. The second says: the time-rate-of-change of momentum is proportional to the force. The third says: action equals reaction. What is momentum? It is the mass times the velocity. It is not the same as velocity. If we exert a certain push on an object that is light, it moves easily. Push just as hard on another object that is much heavier, and it moves much less rapidly. Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia. Now, what is force? This is where the puzzle lies. If a body is accelerating, there is a force on it. That sounds like a definition, and if it were, we would have found out nothing. We could define force to mean mass times acceleration, and physics would be empty. The real content of Newton's laws is that force has independent properties, in addition to F equals m a. Newton himself gave us one such property, gravitation. For everything else, we have to study the forces case by case. The law F equals m a is really a program for studying nature. It tells us that if we study mass times acceleration and call the product force, then we shall find that forces have some simplicity. That is why Newton's law is so powerful. It is a suggestion that forces will be simple. Study any system, find the forces, and the motion follows.

header_title: Why a Rocket Works in Empty Space
tagline: Momentum is conserved piece by piece
audio_script: Newton gave one rule about force: that the forces between interacting bodies are equal and opposite. Action equals reaction. What is meant is this. Suppose we have two small bodies, and the first exerts a force on the second, pushing it with a certain force. Then, simultaneously, the second particle will push on the first with an equal force, in the opposite direction. Furthermore, these forces effectively act in the same line. For the moment let us take it to be true. What is the interesting consequence? If the rate of change of momentum of one particle is always equal and opposite to that of another, then the total momentum does not change. That is the law of conservation of momentum. Now let us verify it experimentally. We use a wonderful invention called an air trough, which gets rid of friction. Blocks of equal mass glide along, supported on air. We place a small explosive cap in a closed cylinder between the two blocks, and set it off. What happens? If the speeds are equal, they should arrive at the ends of the trough at the same time. On reaching the ends they bounce back, and come together and stop at the center where they started. It works. Now suppose we have two equal masses, one moving with velocity v, the other standing still. They collide and stick. What is the resulting velocity? We ride along in a car at velocity minus v. From the car, one mass has zero velocity, the other comes at two v. After collision, the combined mass moves at v, from the car's point of view. Back on the ground, that is v over two. Momentum before was m v. After, it is two m times v over two. Same. The general rule is: the sum of the products of mass and velocity stays the same. This is how a rocket works. It throws mass backward so that it can go forward. There is no air to push against. It pushes against itself.

tagline: PYQ - the definition of average speed
question_text: A car travels 60 km in the first hour and 90 km in the next two hours. What is its average speed over the whole journey?
audio_script: A car travels sixty kilometers in the first hour and ninety kilometers in the next two hours. What is the average speed over the whole journey? The average speed is the total distance divided by the total time. Total distance is sixty plus ninety, one hundred fifty kilometers. Total time is one plus two, three hours. Dividing, we get fifty kilometers per hour. Option A. Notice that we do not simply average the two speeds. If we did, we would get seventy-five kilometers per hour, which is wrong. The car went at different speeds for different amounts of time. So we must weight by time. The correct definition of average speed is total distance divided by total time. This is a simple example, but it is the kind of thing that trips people up when the problem is dressed in more complicated language. For example, if the problem had said the car goes at sixty for one hour and ninety for the next two, and asks for the average, the answer is not the arithmetic mean. It is the weighted mean by time. And if the problem gives speeds but not times, we have to work out the times from the distances. Whenever you see average speed, remember: total distance over total time. That is the definition. Everything else follows from it.

tagline: PYQ - applying Newton's law of gravitation
question_text: Two masses of 4 kg and 9 kg are separated by 3 meters. What is the gravitational force between them? Use G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
audio_script: Two masses of four kilograms and nine kilograms are separated by three meters. What is the gravitational force between them? The constant G is six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven. The formula is F equals G times m one m two, divided by r squared. Substituting, we get six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven, times four times nine, all divided by nine. The nine in the numerator and denominator cancels. So we get six point six seven times ten to the minus eleven, times four. Which is about two point six seven times ten to the minus ten newtons. Option A. Notice how small the gravitational force is between everyday objects. Two masses of a few kilograms, separated by a few meters, attract each other with a force of order ten to the minus ten newtons. That is billions of times smaller than the weight of a grain of sand. Gravity is only noticeable when one of the masses is astronomical. That is why we do not feel the attraction between ourselves and the person sitting next to us. That is why a magnet can pick up a paper clip, but the earth itself cannot. Gravity is a fact about enormous accumulations of matter, not about everyday lumps.
